objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain where aviation weather comes from, read and teach every product and hazard the CFI ACS lists, and coach a student from a raw briefing to a sound go, no-go or divert decision.
why: Weather is where student judgment is weakest and accidents are deadliest; continued VFR flight into IMC is a theme in many fatal accidents [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. Your students will copy how you brief, how you read the numbers and how you say no. On the checkride you must brief, analyze and decide out loud while you teach it.

chunks.title: Where weather comes from, and the briefing your student must learn to build

body.p: Before a flight away from the airport, the pilot in command must become familiar with the weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements and the alternatives if the flight cannot be completed [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]. Your first job is to teach where that weather comes from, so the student knows who made each product and how much to trust it.

head: Source
What it gives the pilot
rows: National Weather Service (NWS)
Weather data, forecasts and warnings for the United States and its waters [[28:19|AWH 2-2]]
Aviation Weather Center (AWC), Kansas City
AIRMETs, SIGMETs, Convective SIGMETs and icing, turbulence and convective products [[28:20|AWH 2-3]]; it runs aviationweather.gov and the GFA [[28:29|AWH 3-6]]
Storm Prediction Center (SPC) and Weather Prediction Center (WPC)
SPC: tornado and severe weather watches. WPC: surface pressure and frontal analyses [[28:20|AWH 2-3]]

Flight Service (1-800-WX-BRIEF, 1800wxbrief.com)
Preflight briefings, flight plans, in-flight advisories and the FAA weather cameras [[28:22|AWH 2-5]] [[28:28|AWH 3-5]]
Commercial providers and apps
Mostly NWS products repackaged with new layout [[28:22|AWH 2-5]]. The FAA does not certify internet weather providers [[28:24|AWH 3-1]]

body.p: A pilot can get a regulatory compliant briefing online without contacting Flight Service. Pilots who do call are encouraged to self-brief first [[28:26|AWH 3-3]]. Flight Service specialists are certified Pilot Weather Briefers: they translate and interpret, but they may not make original forecasts [[28:28|AWH 3-5]]. Every Flight Service briefing, online or by voice, is time-stamped and archived for 45 days [[28:26|AWH 3-3]].

head: Briefing
When to get it
What it is for
rows: Outlook
6 or more hours before departure
Planning only: which weather may be a factor [[37:8|AC 91-92 Table 1]]
Standard
Within 6 hours of the flight
The complete weather picture and its risk factors [[37:8|AC 91-92 Table 1]]

An update on items that may have changed since the standard briefing [[37:8|AC 91-92 Table 1]]

body.p: If departure is more than 2 hours away, a standard briefing leaves out current conditions unless the pilot asks for them [[28:27|AWH 3-4]]. The more doubtful the weather, the more information a pilot needs about the route, runways, destination and alternates [[37:6|AC 91-92 6.3]].

callout.text: AC 91-92 timing to teach: plan ahead with an outlook briefing, get a standard briefing as close to departure as possible, and get an abbreviated briefing just before takeoff if the standard one is 1 hour or more old or the weather is questionable [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].

How to teach it: use the demonstration-performance method. Explain the goal and the order of a briefing, then self-brief a real day out loud while the student watches, then have the student brief the next flight while you supervise, then evaluate together [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Hand the planning to the student as soon as you can and become the mentor [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

check.q: Your student will depart in 3 hours and plans to call Flight Service now for a standard briefing. What will be missing, and what should you teach them to do about it?
check.a: Current conditions will be left out unless the student asks, because departure is more than 2 hours away [[28:27|AWH 3-4]]. Teach them to ask for it, and to get an abbreviated update just before takeoff if the briefing is 1 hour or more old [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].

body.p: Start K2 with the big idea the AIM uses: there are three types of weather information. Observations are raw sensor data, analyses interpret that data, and forecasts predict what will happen [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]]. Reports are observations, so they are the facts the forecasts are checked against.

**Airport observations (METAR and SPECI).** A METAR is the routine report made near the top of the hour. A SPECI is an unscheduled report issued as soon as possible when a set change happens between hourly reports [[28:290|AWH 24-6]].

head: A SPECI is issued when
Threshold
rows: The wind shifts
45° or more in less than 15 minutes, with 10 kt or more throughout [[28:290|AWH 24-6]]
Visibility crosses
3, 2, 1, 1/2 or 1/4 mile, or the lowest standard approach minimum [[28:290|AWH 24-6]]
The ceiling crosses
3,000, 1,500, 1,000 or 500 ft, or the lowest standard approach minimum [[28:290|AWH 24-6]]
Weather begins or ends
Thunderstorm, hail, freezing precipitation, ice pellets, snow, squalls, tornado [[28:290|AWH 24-6]]

bullets: Know who made the report. "AUTO" means no human was involved; augmented reports have an observer adding what the sensors miss [[28:286|AWH 24-2]].
An automated sky condition comes from 30 minutes of sensor data; the other elements use 10 minutes or less [[28:286|AWH 24-2]].
ASOS reports clouds only up to 12,000 ft. Wind direction is true on the internet and FIS-B, but magnetic on the local radio and phone broadcast [[28:287|AWH 24-3]].
AWOS sends a METAR every 20 minutes and does not send SPECIs [[28:288|AWH 24-4]].
An AUTO station cannot report freezing rain or freezing drizzle together with other precipitation. Be alert for icing when it reports snow, or snow and mist, near freezing [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1f]].

body.p: **Pilot observations (PIREP).** Every PIREP has message type, location, time, altitude, aircraft type and at least one weather element. Altitudes are MSL, visibility is in statute miles and time is UTC [[28:310|AWH 24-26]]. The /OV location is where the weather happened, not where the airplane was when the pilot reported it [[28:311|AWH 24-27]]. Tornadoes, severe or extreme turbulence, severe icing, hail, low-level wind shear and volcanic ash make it an urgent PIREP (UUA) [[28:311|AWH 24-27]].

PIREPs are often the most useful icing information because they are facts for a specific time and place [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1]]. Teach students to give them: report good weather as well as bad, and confirm expected conditions as well as surprises [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5]].

callout.text: How to teach it: do not ask "is this METAR VFR?" That is a closed question that tests only rote recall. Ask "what is this report telling you about your flight?" Open-ended why and how questions show you whether the student understands [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

check.q: Your student checks a small airport with AWOS. Its last METAR is 18 minutes old and the student assumes any big change would have produced a SPECI. Correct them.
check.a: AWOS does not send SPECIs; it makes a METAR every 20 minutes [[28:288|AWH 24-4]]. A rapid change will not show until the next one, so listen to the AWOS broadcast or call its phone line for the latest data.

chunks.title: The big picture: surface analysis, the CVA and the Convective Outlook

body.p: **Surface analysis chart.** It shows sea level pressure as isobars, plus highs, lows, ridges, troughs, fronts, drylines and outflow boundaries. The WPC issues it eight times a day, every 3 hours from 00 UTC [[28:350|AWH 25-8]]. A trough is drawn as a dashed line and a ridge as a zigzag line [[28:349|AWH 25-7]]. The symbols on a front point the way it is moving [[28:348|AWH 25-6]].

bullets: Close isobars mean a steep pressure gradient and strong wind; widely spaced isobars mean light wind [[1:296|PHAK 12-12]].
Station plots show wind with barbs: each full barb is 10 kt, a half barb 5 kt and a pennant 50 kt. The arrow points into the wind [[1:296|PHAK 12-12]].
Near the surface, wind crosses the isobars toward low pressure, about 10° over water and up to 45° over rugged terrain [[28:122|AWH 10-7]].
Air converging into a low rises and cools, which favors clouds and precipitation. Air diverging from a high sinks and warms, which favors clearing [[28:150|AWH 12-6]].

body.p: **Ceiling and Visibility Analysis (CVA).** The CVA is a map of current ceiling and visibility by flight category. None of the lesson sources describes the CVA product itself, so teach it from the categories it uses and then show the live map on aviationweather.gov:

head: Flight category (map color)
Ceiling
Visibility
rows: LIFR (purple)
Below 500 ft
and/or below 1 SM [[28:51|AWH 3-28]]
IFR (red)
500 to below 1,000 ft
and/or 1 to below 3 SM [[28:51|AWH 3-28]]
MVFR (blue)
and/or 3 to 5 SM [[28:51|AWH 3-28]]
VFR (green)
Above 3,000 ft
and above 5 SM [[28:51|AWH 3-28]]

body.p: These categories are for situational awareness; they are not the 14 CFR 91.155 VFR minimums [[28:51|AWH 3-28]]. The GFA also has a ceiling and visibility (CIG/VIS) tab for observations and for forecasts [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]] [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4]].

**Convective Outlook (AC).** The SPC issues it for the next eight days. It rates the risk of severe storms (tornado, gusts of 50 kt or more, or hail 1 inch or larger) as marginal, slight, enhanced, moderate or high. Days 1 to 3 also show general thunderstorms (TSTM) [[28:457|AWH 27-56]].

callout.text: How to teach it: make the outlook an outlook-briefing habit, days before a cross-country. Risk mitigation often starts days ahead [[25:14|AIH 1-10]]. On a day with afternoon storms forecast, an early morning departure or waiting until they die out are both real options [[30:40|RMH 5-2]].

check.q: The Day 2 outlook shows only light green (TSTM) over the route. Your student says "no risk area, so storms are not a factor." What do you teach?
check.a: TSTM marks general, non-severe thunderstorms [[28:457|AWH 27-56]]. Any thunderstorm is a hazard: never regard one lightly [[34:119|AIM 7-1-27]]. Plan timing and routing around them.

chunks.title: Forecasts: TAF, GFA and the winds and temperatures aloft (FB)

body.p: **Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF).** A TAF covers the area within 5 SM of the center of the runway complex. NWS TAFs leave out temperature. About 700 airports have one, usually for 24 hours and at some major airports 30 [[28:407|AWH 27-6]]. Scheduled TAFs come out at 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC, and an amended TAF (TAF AMD) replaces the old one at once [[28:409|AWH 27-8]].

head: Group
What the student must say
rows: FM
From this time, a complete new set of conditions replaces everything before it [[28:416|AWH 27-15]] [[28:417|AWH 27-16]]
TEMPO
More than 50% likely, each spell 1 hour or less, adding up to less than half the period [[28:417|AWH 27-16]]
PROB30
A 30% chance of a thunderstorm or precipitation event in that period; the only PROB group in NWS TAFs [[28:418|AWH 27-17]]
Non-convective wind shear from the surface to 2,000 ft; the wind at the top is 270° at 55 kt [[28:416|AWH 27-15]]

body.p: **Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA).** One website for the route between the TAF airports. It shows observations and forecasts from 14 hours in the past to 15 hours ahead: thunderstorms, clouds, flight category, precipitation, icing, turbulence and wind, with wind, icing and turbulence in 3,000 ft steps up to 30,000 ft [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]]. On a slow connection, the static Aviation Cloud Forecast and Aviation Surface Forecast images update every 3 hours and show 3 to 18 hours ahead [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4]]. The GFA Low Altitude mode covers up to 5,000 ft AGL [[28:471|AWH 28-2]].

callout.text: A student can switch GFA layers off, including the AIRMET and SIGMET overlays, and hide hazardous weather on the route [[28:471|AWH 28-2]]. The NDFD forecast on weather.gov can also differ from the GFA for the same place and time [[28:29|AWH 3-6]].

body.p: **Wind and Temperature Aloft Forecast (FB).** Each level reads DDff+TT: direction in tens of degrees true, speed in knots, temperature in °C. 9900 means light and variable or under 5 kt. For 100 to 199 kt, 50 is added to the direction and 100 taken off the speed. No wind is forecast within 1,500 ft of the station elevation and no temperature within 2,500 ft [[28:405|AWH 27-4]]. In the handbook's sample, Kansas City 2130-06 at 12,000 ft decodes as 210° true at 30 kt, minus 6 °C [[28:405|AWH 27-4]].

The FB is coarse. It is updated only four times a day, gives one value for each of three broad time blocks, and its points are about 100 to 150 mi apart [[28:404|AWH 27-3]]. Teach students to interpolate between levels and stations and to look for big shifts in speed or direction [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.7]]. Its temperatures help find icing levels [[37:16|AC 91-92 Appendix A]].

callout.text: How to teach it: decoding is only the understanding level. The goal of aviation instruction is correlation, where the student links what was taught to other blocks of learning [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. So after decoding, ask: does the TAF agree with the GFA, and what do the FB temperatures say about the clouds the TAF forecasts?

check.q: TAF: FM151800 22012KT P6SM BKN040 PROB30 1520/1523 2SM TSRA OVC015CB. Your student plans to arrive at 2130Z and reads it as "good VFR." What do you teach?
check.a: Between 2000Z and 2300Z there is a 30% chance of a thunderstorm with 2 SM in rain and an overcast at 1,500 ft [[28:418|AWH 27-17]]. AC 91-92 says not to plan flights in or near forecast convection [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]], so move the arrival time or plan an alternate.

chunks.title: In-flight aviation weather advisories: AIRMET, SIGMET and Convective SIGMET

body.p: In-flight advisories are forecasts that warn en route aircraft of potentially hazardous weather. There are four types: the SIGMET, the Convective SIGMET, the AIRMET and the Center Weather Advisory (CWA) [[34:68|AIM 7-1-6]] [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]].

head: Advisory
Issued for
Timing
rows: AIRMET (Sierra, Tango, Zulu)

Sierra: IFR and extensive mountain obscuration. Tango: moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 kt or more, low-level wind shear. Zulu: moderate icing and freezing levels [[28:383|AWH 26-16]]
Every 6 hours over the lower 48. Graphics are valid at times no more than 3 hours apart, up to 12 hours ahead [[34:73|AIM 7-1-6]]
SIGMET
Severe icing or severe or extreme turbulence not from thunderstorms; widespread dust or sandstorms below 3 miles; volcanic ash [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]]
Unscheduled; valid 4 hours (6 for tropical cyclones and volcanic ash) [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]]
Convective SIGMET

Severe thunderstorms (surface wind 50 kt or more, hail 3/4 inch or more, or tornadoes), embedded storms, a line of storms, or heavy-precipitation storms over 40% of an area of 3,000 square miles [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]
Hourly at 55 past; the forecast is valid up to 1 hour [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]

callout.text: Any Convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear, even if the text does not say so [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]].

body.p: AIRMETs are meant for all pilots but especially VFR pilots and operators of sensitive aircraft, which is exactly your student in a trainer [[34:73|AIM 7-1-6]]. A SIGMET for severe icing applies to every aircraft, from a small GA airplane to a transport jet [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1d]].

callout.text: No advisory does not mean no hazard. Icing AIRMETs are not issued unless the affected area is large, and a severe icing PIREP does not automatically produce a SIGMET [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1d]]. Check PIREPs too [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1e]].

How to teach it: have the student lay each advisory over the planned route and altitude, then ask "how does this change your plan?" Questions should focus the learner on the decision-making process [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

check.q: Your student says, "SIGMETs are for airliners; AIRMETs are the ones for us." How do you correct that?
check.a: SIGMETs go to all pilots in flight [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]], and a severe icing SIGMET applies to every aircraft from a small GA airplane to a jet [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1d]]. AIRMETs cover lower intensities that matter especially to VFR pilots [[34:73|AIM 7-1-6]].

chunks.title: The atmosphere: composition and stability, temperature and heat exchange, moisture and precipitation

body.p: K3 is the "why" behind every product. On the checkride you will be asked about at least three of its sub-elements, and S2 has you analyze at least three of them on real or given weather. Teach each one as a chain: what it is, what it looks like in the reports, and what it means for this flight.

**Atmospheric composition and stability.** Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, plus argon and a little carbon dioxide; water vapor varies from a trace to about 4% [[28:62|AWH 4-2]]. Almost all weather happens in the troposphere, which averages about 36,000 ft deep [[28:63|AWH 4-3]]. Stability is the air's resistance to vertical motion. In stable air small disturbances die out; in unstable air they grow into turbulence, tall clouds and severe weather [[1:296|PHAK 12-12]].

head: Rising air parcel
Cools at about
Dewpoint drops about
rows: Unsaturated (dry adiabatic)
Saturated, in cloud (moist adiabatic)
1.2 to 3 °C per 1,000 ft; the handbook uses 2 °C [[28:147|AWH 12-3]]
The same rate as the temperature [[28:147|AWH 12-3]]

bullets: Absolute stability: the actual lapse rate is less than the moist rate, including isothermal layers and inversions [[28:155|AWH 13-2]].
Conditional instability: the lapse rate is between the moist and dry rates. Virtually all showers and thunderstorms form in this kind of air [[28:158|AWH 13-5]] [[28:257|AWH 22-2]].
Absolute instability: the lapse rate is greater than the dry rate [[28:157|AWH 13-4]].
Daytime heating lowers stability; nighttime cooling raises it [[28:162|AWH 13-9]].

Air moving over a warmer surface becomes unstable: cumulus, showers, turbulence, good visibility. Over a colder surface it becomes stable: stratus, fog and poor visibility from trapped particles [[1:302|PHAK 12-18]].

body.p: **Temperature and heat exchange.** Heat moves by radiation [[28:70|AWH 5-4]], by conduction from one substance to another [[28:72|AWH 5-6]], and by convection inside moving air; because air conducts heat poorly, convection does most of the work [[28:73|AWH 5-7]]. Water also absorbs or releases latent heat when it changes state [[28:85|AWH 6-6]]. Water warms and cools much more slowly than land, which softens temperature swings near large lakes and oceans [[28:76|AWH 5-10]]. The coldest time of day is usually shortly after sunrise and the warmest is midafternoon; the daily swing is largest over land with clear skies, dry air and light wind [[28:94|AWH 7-8]]. The standard lapse rate is 6.5 °C per km, but the real value seldom matches it [[28:77|AWH 5-11]]. On clear, calm nights the ground cools fastest and a surface inversion forms [[28:78|AWH 5-12]]; the inversion acts as a lid that traps haze, smoke and fog below it [[1:297|PHAK 12-13]].

**Moisture and precipitation.** As the temperature-dewpoint spread shrinks, relative humidity rises; at zero spread the air is saturated. The surface spread helps you anticipate fog but says little about precipitation, which needs saturated layers aloft [[28:84|AWH 6-5]]. Every 20 °F of warming doubles how much water the air can hold [[1:297|PHAK 12-13]]. Significant precipitation usually needs clouds at least 4,000 ft thick, so expect thicker clouds at an airport reporting light or heavier precipitation [[28:166|AWH 14-2]]. Ice pellets at the surface mean an inversion, with freezing rain at a higher altitude [[1:301|PHAK 12-17]].

In the figure, the surface air is 18 °C with a dewpoint of 13 °C. Rising, it closes the spread by 2.5 °C per 1,000 ft, so it saturates at 2,000 ft, the lifted condensation level, and the cloud base forms there [[28:147|AWH 12-3]]. PHAK gives the same rule in Fahrenheit: divide the spread by 4.4 and multiply by 1,000 for the base in feet AGL [[1:298|PHAK 12-14]].

callout.text: How to teach it: cover the parcel column above 1,000 ft and have the student predict each row before you reveal it. Asking them to work it out, rather than read it, moves them from rote recall toward application [[25:65|AIH 3-14]].

check.q: In the figure, why does the parcel cool only 2 °C per 1,000 ft above 2,000 ft instead of 3?
check.a: It is saturated. Condensation releases latent heat that offsets part of the cooling, so it cools at the moist rate, which the handbook rounds to 2 °C per 1,000 ft [[28:147|AWH 12-3]].

chunks.title: Weather system formation: air masses, fronts and clouds

body.p: **Weather system formation, including air masses and fronts.** An air mass takes on the temperature and moisture of the region where it sits: continental (dry) or maritime (moist), and arctic, polar or tropical. The common five are cA, cP, cT, mP and mT [[28:135|AWH 11-2]]. When two air masses meet, the boundary is a front, and an approaching front always means a change in the weather [[1:302|PHAK 12-18]].

head: Front
Speed
Typical weather
rows: Warm
10 to 25 mph, gentle slope [[28:138|AWH 11-5]]
Cirriform or stratiform clouds and fog ahead of it; thunderstorms are likely in summer [[1:302|PHAK 12-18]]
Cold

Narrow band of weather. Unstable warm air gives showers and thunderstorms, and a squall line may form along or ahead of it. Behind it: clearing, gusty turbulent wind, colder air [[28:139|AWH 11-6]] [[1:304|PHAK 12-20]]
Stationary
Little movement; can last for days [[28:140|AWH 11-7]]
A mix of warm front and cold front weather [[28:140|AWH 11-7]]
Occluded
A cold front catches a warm front [[28:141|AWH 11-8]]
Warm front weather followed right away by cold front weather; unstable air can bring embedded thunderstorms [[28:141|AWH 11-8]]

body.p: Clues a cold front is near: a high dewpoint and falling pressure. As it passes, pressure bottoms out and then rises, the temperature and dewpoint drop fast and the wind becomes variable and gusty [[1:304|PHAK 12-20]]. Wind shifts are most pronounced with cold fronts [[1:305|PHAK 12-21]].

This figure is a ready-made correlation lesson. Ahead of the front, Pittsburgh has 3 SM in smoke and Columbus 6 SM in haze, both with a wind from 200°. Indianapolis, at the front, has thunderstorms and heavy rain, a 1,000 ft overcast and a dewpoint only 1 °C below the temperature. St. Louis, behind it, has a northwest wind of 18 kt, 10 SM and a dewpoint of 2 °C [[1:305|PHAK 12-21]]. The PHAK's advice for this flight is to wait at Indianapolis until the front passes [[1:304|PHAK 12-20]].

**Clouds.** There are four basic forms. Cirriform clouds form above 20,000 ft and are mostly ice. Nimbus clouds, usually 7,000 to 15,000 ft, bring steady precipitation. Cumuliform clouds show rising air and have flat bases. Stratiform clouds are featureless layers, often only a few hundred feet up [[28:152|AWH 12-8]]. Low clouds have bases from the surface to about 6,500 ft [[28:153|AWH 12-9]]. Air is lifted to make clouds by terrain, by friction, by fronts and by buoyancy [[28:149|AWH 12-5]]. A ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, or the vertical visibility into an obscuration [[1:301|PHAK 12-17]].

callout.text: Cloud shape tells you stability: heaped cumuliform clouds mean rising, unstable air; flat stratiform layers mean stable air [[28:152|AWH 12-8]] [[1:302|PHAK 12-18]].

check.q: Using the figure, which METAR shows the front has already passed, and what proves it?
check.a: St. Louis. The wind has shifted to the northwest at 18 kt, the temperature and dewpoint have dropped to 8 and 2 °C, visibility is 10 SM and the altimeter is higher than at Indianapolis [[1:305|PHAK 12-21]]. After cold front passage, pressure rises, temperatures stay cool and visibility improves [[1:304|PHAK 12-20]].

body.p: **Wind (windshear, mountain wave, factors affecting wind).** Pressure gradient force pushes air from high to low pressure, and the closer the isobars the stronger the wind [[28:117|AWH 10-2]]. The Coriolis force turns moving air [[28:118|AWH 10-3]]. Friction slows the wind near the ground and turns it across the isobars. About 2,000 ft AGL the wind is usually 20° to 40° to the right of the surface wind and stronger [[1:296|PHAK 12-12]].

bullets: Windshear: non-convective low-level wind shear is a change of 10 kt or more per 100 ft, in a layer more than 200 ft thick, within 2,000 ft of the surface. Look for it with passing fronts, temperature inversions and winds aloft above 25 kt. Shear that changes airspeed more than 15 kt or vertical speed more than 500 fpm is often called severe [[28:240|AWH 19-8]].
Mountain wave: it needs strong wind across a ridge and stable air; unstable air builds convective clouds instead. The worst events come from late autumn to early spring [[28:191|AWH 16-2]].
A rotor zone often forms near or below ridge level on the downwind side, under a wave crest [[28:199|AWH 16-10]].

With 20 kt or more at ridge level, low flight over mountains can bring moderate or greater turbulence, strong up and downdrafts and rotors [[28:242|AWH 19-10]]. Lenticular and rotor clouds prove a wave exists, but they may be missing if the air is dry [[28:205|AWH 16-16]].

body.p: **Turbulence.** It comes from convective currents, from obstructions to the wind (mechanical turbulence) and from wind shear [[28:234|AWH 19-2]]. Convective turbulence is bumpy under and in cumulus clouds and usually smooth above them; dry thermals give no visual warning [[28:234|AWH 19-2]]. Mechanical turbulence grows with wind speed, surface roughness, obstruction size and stability [[28:236|AWH 19-4]].

head: Intensity
What the pilot feels
rows: Light
Slight, erratic changes in altitude or attitude [[28:233|AWH 19-1]]
Moderate
Changes in altitude or attitude, but the airplane stays in positive control [[28:233|AWH 19-1]]
Severe
Large, abrupt changes; large airspeed variations [[28:233|AWH 19-1]]
Extreme
Violently tossed about; practically impossible to control [[28:233|AWH 19-1]]

body.p: In extremely rough air, such as thunderstorms or fronts, slow to the design maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

callout.text: How to teach it: after a bumpy lesson, have the student rate the ride on this scale and give it to you as a PIREP. It turns a definition into something they own, and PIREPs help everyone [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5]].

check.q: Winds at ridge level are 25 kt across a ridge in stable air, but the sky is clear with no lenticulars. Your student says no clouds means no wave. Reply.
check.a: Wave clouds can be absent when the air is dry [[28:205|AWH 16-16]]. With 20 kt or more at ridge level, expect turbulence, strong downdrafts and rotors downwind [[28:242|AWH 19-10]].

body.p: **Thunderstorms.** A thunderstorm needs three ingredients: enough water vapor, unstable air and a lifting mechanism such as converging winds, a front, upslope flow or an old storm's outflow. A cell lives about 30 minutes, and its updrafts can exceed 3,000 fpm [[28:257|AWH 22-2]].

bullets: There is no useful link between how a storm looks and how much turbulence or hail it holds. Severe turbulence can extend 20 miles from a severe storm, about 10 miles from a less severe one [[34:119|AIM 7-1-26]].
No path between strong radar echoes 20 to 30 miles apart or less can be considered free of severe turbulence [[34:119|AIM 7-1-26]].
Lightning strikes on aircraft are most likely between minus 5 and plus 5 °C [[34:119|AIM 7-1-26]].
Hail may fall in clear air several miles from the cloud [[1:309|PHAK 12-25]].

body.p: **Microbursts.** A microburst is the most severe type of wind shear. A typical one is less than 2.5 mi across and about 1,000 ft deep, and it lasts 5 to 15 minutes. Its downdrafts reach 6,000 fpm, with headwind gains and losses of 30 to 90 kt. Virga or a ring of blowing dust may be the only visible clue [[28:263|AWH 22-8]]. If you meet one, expect more [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

head: Avoidance rule to teach
Source
rows: Do not take off or land with a thunderstorm approaching; do not fly under one or under its anvil
Avoid any severe storm or intense echo by at least 20 miles
Go around the whole area if it has 6/10 thunderstorm coverage
Treat any storm with tops of 35,000 ft or higher as extremely hazardous; vivid, frequent lightning suggests a severe storm
If you cannot get around them, divert and wait them out on the ground
Do not plan flights in or near current or forecast convection

callout.text: How to teach it: walk the student through the figure from 1 to 5 before they ever see a summer afternoon cross-country. The first headwind actually improves performance; everything after it, from point 2 to point 5, takes performance away [[34:109|AIM 7-1-24]].

check.q: Your student points to two light-green cells 15 miles apart on a NEXRAD picture and wants to fly between them. What do you teach?
check.a: Never regard a thunderstorm lightly, even with light echoes [[34:119|AIM 7-1-27]]. No path between strong echoes 20 to 30 miles apart or less is free of severe turbulence [[34:119|AIM 7-1-26]], and data-link NEXRAD is for avoiding the whole area, not threading it [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]].

chunks.title: Icing and the freezing level, frost, fog and mist, and obstructions to visibility

body.p: **Icing and freezing level information.** Cloud droplets can stay liquid far below 0 °C. From 0 to minus 10 °C clouds are mostly supercooled water, from minus 10 to minus 20 °C water and ice mix, and below minus 20 °C they are usually ice crystals [[28:244|AWH 20-2]]. Expect icing in any cloud at or below 0 °C [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]]. About half of icing reports fall between minus 8 and minus 12 °C, and the peak is near 10,000 ft [[28:245|AWH 20-3]].

bullets: The freezing level is the lowest altitude where the air reaches 0 °C. The freezing level graphics update hourly and mark places with more than one freezing level aloft [[28:365|AWH 25-23]].
The winds aloft forecast gives the approximate freezing level [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]]. Know it and any inversions so you have a way out of ice [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1c]].
In stratiform clouds, icing is usually in a layer 3,000 to 4,000 ft thick, so a climb or descent of a few thousand feet may clear it [[28:246|AWH 20-4]].
Freezing rain below a front can cause severe clear icing; ice pellets at the surface mean icing above [[28:247|AWH 20-5]].

An airplane certificated for IFR is not necessarily certificated for icing; check the AFM or POH [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4]]. Pilots of airplanes not certificated for icing must avoid it and exit at once if they meet it [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]].
First move in ice: leave the visible moisture by descending below the bases, climbing above the tops or turning [[28:249|AWH 20-7]].

body.p: **Frost.** Frost forms on an airplane parked outside on a clear night when moist air meets a skin cooled below freezing by radiation [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4b]]. Frost, snow or ice no thicker or rougher than coarse sandpaper can cut lift 30% and raise drag up to 40% [[28:249|AWH 20-7]]. Remove all of it before flight. A heated hangar works, but the airplane must be dry before it goes back outside or the water will refreeze [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a]].

**Fog and mist.** Fog is a cloud at the surface that cuts visibility below 5/8 SM. It seldom forms when the spread is more than 2 °C [[28:222|AWH 18-2]]; AC 91-92 tells pilots to be especially cautious at 3 °C or less [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]. Mist is the lighter version, with visibility from 5/8 SM to less than 7 SM [[28:229|AWH 18-9]].

head: Fog type
How it forms
Clues
rows: Radiation
Ground cools the air on clear nights with little wind [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]]
Low-lying areas; burns off as the sun warms; ground fog if under 20 ft thick [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]]
Advection
Warm, moist air moves over a cold surface [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]]
Needs wind; deepens up to about 15 kt, lifts into low stratus above that [[28:224|AWH 18-4]]
Upslope
Moist, stable air forced up sloping land [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]]
Needs wind; may last for days [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]]
Steam
Cold, dry air over warm water [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]]
Low-level turbulence and icing are common [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]]

body.p: Expected climate matters: the West Coast is prone to advection fog from cold offshore water, and in winter Gulf moisture spreading over cold ground can carry it as far north as the Great Lakes [[28:225|AWH 18-5]].
**Obstructions to visibility (smoke, haze, volcanic ash).**

bullets: Haze forms in stable air, usually a few thousand feet thick. Above it air-to-air visibility is good, but slant visibility toward the ground is poor, and worse facing the sun [[28:229|AWH 18-9]].
Smoke can carry carbon monoxide, and haze and smoke clear more slowly than fog because the air must move them away [[28:229|AWH 18-9]].
In dust, slant visibility is usually worse than the reported surface visibility [[28:230|AWH 18-10]].
Volcanic ash is hard to see at night or in cloud and radar cannot detect fine ash [[28:231|AWH 18-11]]. It can badly damage piston engines and sandblast the windshield [[28:232|AWH 18-12]].
A valley station may report a VFR ceiling while the mountains around it are in fog [[28:232|AWH 18-12]].

check.q: At dusk your destination reports 12/10 with a light wind and a clear sky, and a front brought rain there this morning. What do you want the student to predict?
check.a: A 2 °C spread is right at the edge where fog forms, and AC 91-92 flags 3 °C or less [[28:222|AWH 18-2]] [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]. Clear skies and little wind favor radiation fog as the ground cools overnight [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]], so plan to land well before dark or pick an alternate.

chunks.title: Risk: cockpit weather displays and the limits of every weather source

body.p: **Flight deck instrument displays of digital weather and aeronautical information.** FIS-B is the free FAA broadcast on the 978 MHz UAT link. An aircraft gets it only within range and line of sight of a ground station [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]]. It carries AIRMETs, SIGMETs, Convective SIGMETs, METARs, NEXRAD, NOTAMs, PIREPs, TAFs, winds aloft, lightning, turbulence, icing, cloud tops and CWAs [[37:13|AC 91-92 7.7]] [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]], but not every product or NOTAM a preflight briefing includes [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]].

head: Display fact
Why it matters
rows: The NEXRAD age label shows the age of the mosaic, not of the weather in it
The weather can be 15 to 20 minutes older than the label [[1:329|PHAK 13-19]]
CONUS NEXRAD is sent every 15 minutes; regional NEXRAD every 2.5 minutes [[34:83|AIM TBL 7-1-3]]
A picture can be stale before it even arrives
Low-altitude-tier ground radios do not send CONUS NEXRAD, only regional NEXRAD with a 150 NM look-ahead [[34:84|AIM TBL 7-1-4]]
Low and slow, you may not see weather beyond about 150 NM
NEXRAD resolution is 1.24 miles, and base reflectivity cannot tell hail from rain or show cloud layers [[1:331|PHAK 13-21]]
Zoomed in, the blocks look precise but are not
FIS-B NOTAMs older than 30 days are not sent, except TFRs [[34:82|AIM 7-1-9]]
The PIC still must review everything before flight
Symbols, ranges and modes come from the avionics manufacturer [[34:84|AIM 7-1-9]]
Teach the box in the airplane you fly

body.p: **Installed onboard weather equipment.** Airborne weather radar is for avoiding severe weather, not for penetrating it [[28:275|AWH 22-20]]. It cannot detect clear-air turbulence and does not keep you out of cloud, and a strong cell can absorb the beam and hide cells behind it (attenuation) [[28:276|AWH 22-21]]. Its latency is minimal, unlike NEXRAD [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]. Data-link NEXRAD on a display is not onboard radar.

head: Aviation weather reports and forecasts
Built-in limit
rows: METAR
One point. A station near VFR minimums does not mean the route is VFR; areas en route may be below [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]
TAF
Only the 5 SM around the runway complex [[28:407|AWH 27-6]]
FB
Four issues a day and one value per broad time block [[28:404|AWH 27-3]]
Icing PIREP
Subjective and aircraft-specific: a 747 may report light icing in conditions that are severe for a Mooney [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3]]
Any forecast
It carries uncertainty, which grows the further ahead it reaches [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]

body.p: **Inflight weather resources.** ASOS and AWOS broadcasts reach about 25 NM; ATIS and Flight Service are also on the radio [[28:30|AWH 3-7]]. Controllers advise of hazardous weather within 150 NM of their sector [[28:22|AWH 2-5]]. ATC radar cannot see clouds or turbulence and calls everything "precipitation" [[34:97|AIM 7-1-12]]. Flight Service specialists can see NEXRAD, echo tops and more [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]].

callout.text: AIM rules for FIS: it is not the sole source of weather; it supports strategic decisions 20 minutes or more ahead, never tactical moves under 3 minutes; when it differs from ATC or Flight Service, use the most recent data from the most authoritative source; and too many layers raise workload, especially single pilot [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]].

How to teach it: data-link weather is an advantage only if the pilot is trained to retrieve and evaluate it without losing situational awareness [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]. Teach the display on the ground, then in flight with the student flying and you watching their scan.

check.q: Your student says, "The NEXRAD says 2 minutes old, so that cell is where it shows." Correct them.
check.a: The label gives the age of the mosaic, not the weather; the weather can be 15 to 20 minutes older [[1:329|PHAK 13-19]]. NEXRAD shows where the weather was, so use it only to avoid whole areas [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]].

chunks.title: Risk: go, no-go and divert decisions

body.p: Teach the decision points, not just the first one. The easiest time to cancel for weather is before walking out to the airplane; the second easiest is just before takeoff [[25:20|AIH 1-16]]. Then review again at the midpoint, hourly on flights over 2 hours, before descent and before the pattern. Pilots who wait until the ATIS is in range have left many good options behind them [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

**Personal weather minimums.** What is legal and what is smart for this pilot are different things [[25:9|AIH 1-5]]. The RMH builds minimums in steps: learn the flight categories, list recent experience, then record the lowest conditions comfortably flown [[30:13|RMH 2-1]]. Its sample baseline is a day VFR ceiling of 2,500 ft with 4 miles, a night ceiling of 5,000 ft with 8 miles, and wind limits of 10 kt, 5 kt gusts and a 7 kt crosswind [[30:16|RMH 2-4]].

head: If you face
Adjust the baseline by at least
rows: Pilot: illness, medication, stress, fatigue, lack of currency
Adding 500 ft to the ceiling [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]
Aircraft: unfamiliar airplane or avionics
Adding 1/2 mile to visibility [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]
Environment: unfamiliar airport, airspace or terrain
Adding 500 ft to runway length [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]
External pressures: must-meet deadlines, passengers
Subtracting 5 kt from wind limits [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]

body.p: With several conditions, adjust for each. The RMH example, a night cross-country to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday, adds 1,000 ft to the ceiling, 1 mile to visibility and 1,000 ft to runway length. Never adjust minimums to complete a specific flight, change only one variable at a time, and see a flight instructor before a big change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. If items are marginal in two or more risk categories, do not go [[25:206|AIH D-1]].

**Hazardous weather conditions, including known or forecast icing or turbulence aloft.** Ask the AIH environment questions: Is there icing, current or forecast? What is the spread and the temperature at altitude? Can a descent be made safely all along the route? Are strong winds over mountains forecast, which can cause severe turbulence even with no other weather? [[25:9|AIH 1-5]]. An airplane not certificated for icing must avoid it [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]]. Severe turbulence and severe icing bring SIGMETs [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]].
**Circumstances that would make diversion prudent.** Teach these triggers and plan the outs before takeoff:

bullets: Weather lowering below personal limits en route: wait it out or turn around; never continue VFR into IMC [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].
Weather different from the forecast: have alternatives and be ready and willing to divert [[25:9|AIH 1-5]].
An area of thunderstorms you cannot get around: divert and wait on the ground [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]].
Ice building in an airplane not certificated for it: exit as fast as possible and declare an emergency to ATC [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]].

A system malfunction or poor planning can also force a diversion, so check the charts for airports along the route before every cross-country [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. In marginal weather, pick an alternate for every 25 to 30 NM of the route [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]] [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]].

callout.text: A numerical FRAT can mislead. A line of embedded thunderstorms on the route may be the only risk listed, so the score says "go" [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]. A "VFR flight not recommended" statement is advisory; the decision still belongs to the pilot [[28:26|AWH 3-3]].

check.q: Your student's day VFR minimum is a 3,000 ft ceiling. The trip is tomorrow, a client is waiting, and the forecast is 2,700 ft. The student wants to lower the minimum "just this once." What do you teach?
check.a: No. Minimums are never adjusted to complete a specific flight; that is done when there is no pressure [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Delay, choose another way to travel or cancel, and tell the client early [[30:40|RMH 5-2]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: brief, analyze, decide

body.p: The checkride Skills say you demonstrate and explain at the same time. So practice teaching weather as a lesson with a beginning, middle and end.

head: Phase
What you do
Source
rows: Explain
Before the lesson: the objective, the standard and the order of a standard briefing
Demonstrate
Self-brief a real day out loud: adverse conditions, synopsis, current conditions, en route forecast, destination forecast, winds aloft, NOTAMs. If you get off track, say so
Student performs
The student briefs the next flight soon after your demonstration while you supervise
Evaluate
Collaborative critique: replay, reconstruct, reflect, redirect; then compare your assessment with theirs

body.p: **S1, the briefing.** Students first write down the flight: VFR or IFR, aircraft, departure, route, destination and alternates, altitudes, departure time and time en route [[37:9|AC 91-92 7.4]]. Then they review weather in the logical order of climbout, en route and descent [[37:10|AC 91-92 7.4.1.5]], and the destination from 1 hour before to 1 hour after arrival [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.6]].

**S2, the analysis.** For at least three K3 conditions, teach the chain: what the product shows, what it means, what you will do. For example: the spread gives the cloud base [[28:146|AWH 12-2]]; the FB temperatures give the freezing level [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]]; a cold front on the chart warns of a narrow band of showers and gusty wind behind it [[28:139|AWH 11-6]].
**S3, the decision.** The student compares the picture with personal minimums and PAVE, and states a decision with a reason and a plan B [[25:8|AIH 1-4]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

bullets: Build it in blocks: in pre-solo training, demonstrate a non-numerical risk tool and have the student able to do a basic risk analysis by first solo; in cross-country training, require a full analysis for every flight and review it as you would their navigation log [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

Use real, local weather. Scenarios work best when they match the weather and terrain the learner will actually meet [[25:157|AIH 7-13]]. Plan possible in-flight changes into the scenario [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].
Grade the decision, not just the decoding: explain, practice, then manage and decide without you [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].
If a learner keeps canceling on good-weather days, ask why; it may be worry about the lesson, not the weather [[25:28|AIH 1-24]].

callout.text: Risk of teaching it: an unprepared learner is a serious hazard. A syllabus, good ground instruction and a thorough briefing before each flight are part of your risk control [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

check.q: Your student decoded every product perfectly but could not say whether to go. What learning level have they reached, and what is your next step?
check.a: Understanding, maybe application, but not correlation, which is the goal of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Next, give a scenario and ask open-ended questions that make them link the products to a decision [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

body.p: These are the weather errors the sources warn about. Watch for each one during briefings and in flight.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Using cockpit weather tactically
The student plans to "pick a way through" cells on the NEXRAD display
Teach strategic use only, 20 minutes or more ahead, to avoid the whole area [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]] [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]
Trusting the reporting stations for the whole route
"Both airports are VFR, so the route is VFR"
Areas en route can be below VFR even when stations are at or near VFR minimums [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]
A stale briefing
The standard briefing is hours old at engine start
Get an abbreviated update if it is 1 hour or more old or the weather is questionable [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]]
Hiding hazards on the screen
GFA layers or AIRMET and SIGMET overlays switched off
Show what is turned off and why it can hide hazardous weather [[28:471|AWH 28-2]]
"No advisory, no ice"
The student skips PIREPs because no icing AIRMET is posted
Icing AIRMETs need a large area; read the PIREPs [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1d]] [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1e]]
Misreading a PIREP
Reads /OV as the airplane's position, or a jet's "light" icing as light for a trainer
/OV is where the weather was [[28:311|AWH 24-27]]; icing PIREPs are aircraft-specific [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3]]
Bending minimums for the trip
"Just this once" with a deadline or passengers waiting
Never adjust minimums for a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]
Late weather updates in flight
Waits for the destination ATIS to check weather
Review the plan at the midpoint and hourly on long flights [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]
Going on top
Plans to climb over a layer hoping for a hole at the destination
Do not proceed on top hoping for a hole or for ATC to talk you down [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]
Waiting too long to ask for help
Hesitates to call ATC when the weather closes in
Do not hesitate to declare an emergency when safety is at risk [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]

callout.text: Fix errors with questions, not lectures: "Where did that report come from? How old is it? What would make you turn around?" Effective questions focus the learner on decision-making [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

check.q: In cruise, your student says the destination ATIS will be in range in 20 minutes and they will check the weather then. What error is this, and what should they do?
check.a: Waiting for the ATIS leaves good options behind. Do the 5P review at the midpoint, hourly on longer flights, and get updates from Flight Service or FIS now [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

scenario.title: Coaching a student's first solo cross-country weather call
scenario.setup: It is late October. Your student pilot plans a solo cross-country of about 90 NM east, departing at 1300 local and returning by 1600. At 0700 the airplane sits outside with frost on the wings. The surface chart shows a cold front 250 miles west of your home airport, moving east at about 25 mph. The destination TAF has PROB30 TSRA for 1700 to 2000 local. The FB at 6,000 ft is 2425+05 and at 9,000 ft 2530-01. The student's written day VFR minimum is a 3,000 ft ceiling and 5 miles. You will teach the decision, not make it for them.

questions.q: At 0700 the student asks for a "briefing for today." Which briefing type, and what follows before departure?
questions.a: Departure is 6 hours away, so an outlook briefing now [[37:8|AC 91-92 Table 1]], then a standard briefing as close to departure as possible, and an abbreviated update if that one is 1 hour or more old at takeoff [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].

questions.q: Where is the front likely to be at 1600, and why does that matter?
questions.a: At about 25 mph it covers roughly 225 of its 250 miles in the 9 hours from 0700 to 1600, so it will be only about 25 miles west of the home airport as the student returns (application). Cold fronts can bring a narrow band of showers and thunderstorms, a squall line along or ahead of them, and gusty, turbulent wind behind [[28:139|AWH 11-6]].

questions.q: What does the PROB30 group tell the student about the return leg?
questions.a: A 30% chance of thunderstorms at the destination from 1700 to 2000 local [[28:418|AWH 27-17]]. That is after the planned 1600 return, but there is no margin for a late departure, and AC 91-92 says not to plan near forecast convection [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

questions.q: What freezing level do the FB temperatures suggest, and does it matter on this flight?
questions.a: It falls 6 °C in 3,000 ft, so 0 °C is about 2,500 ft above 6,000, near 8,500 ft (application). The FB gives the approximate freezing level [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]]. A low VFR cruise stays below it, but showers near the front would put any cloud above that level in icing range [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]].

questions.q: What must happen to the frost before the 1300 departure?
questions.a: All of it must be removed; even a sandpaper-rough layer can cut lift 30% and raise drag up to 40% [[28:249|AWH 20-7]]. If the airplane goes in a heated hangar, it must be dry before it comes back out [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a]].

questions.q: At the standard briefing the destination forecast drops to a 2,800 ft ceiling. How do you guide the student's decision?
questions.a: Ask open-ended questions so the student finds it: what is your minimum, and what does the forecast say? [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. The forecast is below the written 3,000 ft minimum, and minimums are never lowered for a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. The right call is to delay or cancel [[30:40|RMH 5-2]].

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to "use available aviation weather resources to obtain an adequate weather briefing." The examiner watches you self-brief a real or given flight in the standard order, name the source and age of each product, and say why you would update it before takeoff [[37:9|AC 91-92 7.4]] [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].
skills.practice: Brief a real flight every day for a week out loud, as if a student were beside you. Time yourself and cover all seven standard briefing elements.

skills.do: The ACS says you "analyze the implications of at least three of the conditions listed in K3a through K3l, using actual weather or weather conditions provided by the evaluator." For each condition, state the product, what it shows and what it means for the flight, for example cloud bases from the spread or the freezing level from the FB [[28:146|AWH 12-2]] [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]].
skills.practice: Pick three different K3 conditions each day from the live weather and write the product, meaning and action chain for each.

skills.do: The ACS says you "correlate weather information to make a go/no-go decision." The examiner wants a clear decision, the reasons from the weather, how it compares with personal minimums, and a plan B, taught the way you would teach a student [[30:17|RMH 2-5]] [[25:8|AIH 1-4]].
skills.practice: Role-play with another applicant who plays a student pushing to go. Lead them to the decision with questions, then run a collaborative critique.

quiz.q: Which of these may NOT make an original weather forecast?
options: A Flight Service specialist
An NWS Weather Forecast Office forecaster
An Aviation Weather Center forecaster
A Center Weather Service Unit meteorologist
quiz.why: Flight Service specialists are certified Pilot Weather Briefers who translate and interpret forecasts but may not make original ones [[28:28|AWH 3-5]].

quiz.q: In an automated (AUTO) METAR, the sky condition is built from sensor data gathered over the last:
options: 2 minutes
10 minutes
30 minutes
60 minutes
quiz.why: Automated sky condition uses the 30 minutes ending at the observation time; other elements use 10 minutes or less [[28:286|AWH 24-2]].

quiz.q: On a surface analysis chart, a zigzag line marks a:
options: Trough
Ridge
Dryline
Stationary front
quiz.why: A ridge, an elongated area of relatively high pressure, is drawn as a zigzag; a trough is a dashed line [[28:349|AWH 25-7]].

quiz.q: A TEMPO group in a TAF describes conditions that are:
options: Expected to replace everything before them from a set time
More than 50% likely, lasting 1 hour or less each time and less than half the period in total
A 30% chance of thunderstorms or precipitation
Forecast only for the area 5 to 10 SM from the airport
quiz.why: TEMPO is for temporary changes with greater than 50% probability, each lasting 1 hour or less and adding up to less than half the period [[28:417|AWH 27-16]].

quiz.q: An FB station sits at 1,000 ft MSL. Why does its 3,000 ft level show a wind but no temperature?
options: Temperatures are never forecast below 6,000 ft at any station
No temperature is forecast within 2,500 ft of the station elevation
The temperature is the same as the surface report
The wind is light and variable
quiz.why: Wind is not forecast within 1,500 ft of the station elevation and temperature not within 2,500 ft [[28:405|AWH 27-4]].

quiz.q: A Convective SIGMET's forecast is valid for up to:
options: 1 hour
2 hours
4 hours
6 hours
quiz.why: Convective SIGMETs are issued hourly at 55 past and the forecast is valid for up to 1 hour [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]].

quiz.q: The actual lapse rate in a layer is greater than the dry adiabatic rate. The layer is:
options: Absolutely stable
Neutral
Conditionally unstable
Absolutely unstable
quiz.why: A lapse rate greater than the dry adiabatic rate (superadiabatic) means absolute instability [[28:157|AWH 13-4]].

quiz.q: The AIM says lightning strikes on aircraft are most likely at temperatures between:
options: Minus 20 and minus 10 °C
Minus 5 and plus 5 °C
Plus 5 and plus 15 °C
Minus 40 and minus 20 °C
quiz.why: Strikes are most likely between minus 5 and plus 5 °C, and can happen in clear air near a storm [[34:119|AIM 7-1-26]].

quiz.q: Through a low-altitude-tier FIS-B ground radio, what NEXRAD does your student receive?
options: CONUS and regional NEXRAD
CONUS NEXRAD only
Regional NEXRAD only, with a 150 NM look-ahead
No NEXRAD at all
quiz.why: Low-altitude-tier radios do not provide CONUS NEXRAD; regional NEXRAD comes with a 150 NM look-ahead [[34:84|AIM TBL 7-1-4]].

quiz.q: Using the AIH Personal Minimums Checklist, a pilot finds marginal items in two risk categories. The checklist says:
options: Go, but brief the passengers
Go if the weather is VFR
Raise the minimums by 500 ft and go
Do not go
quiz.why: Be wary of one marginal item; with marginal items in two or more risk categories, do not go [[25:206|AIH D-1]].

final_quiz.q: Your student needs only an update on one item before departure. Per AC 91-92, what should an abbreviated briefing still check?
options: Only the item the pilot asked about
Adverse conditions along the route, changes since the last briefing and TFR updates
The full standard briefing again
Winds aloft and NOTAMs only
final_quiz.why: Even for specific information, check updates to adverse conditions, changes since the previous briefing and TFR updates [[37:12|AC 91-92 7.5]] [[37:13|AC 91-92 7.5]].

final_quiz.q: A PIREP reads UA /OV ABC090020/TM 1530/FL060/TP C172/TB MOD. Where was the turbulence?
options: Over the ABC VOR
20 NM east of ABC, on the 090 radial
90 NM from ABC on the 020 radial
Wherever the Cessna was when it called
final_quiz.why: The location is identifier, three digits of radial and three of distance: 090° at 20 NM. /OV is where the weather occurred, not where the airplane was when reporting [[28:311|AWH 24-27]].

final_quiz.q: A TAF period starts FM152100 with a new wind, visibility and clouds but no weather group. The period before it had -RA. What should your student expect after 2100Z?
options: Light rain continues, since only changed items are listed
No significant weather is forecast; an FM group is complete on its own
Rain is possible 30% of the time
The forecaster forgot the weather group
final_quiz.why: Everything after an FM group replaces what came before, and every element is included; the weather group is left out only when none is expected [[28:416|AWH 27-15]] [[28:417|AWH 27-16]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's GFA picture shows no turbulence or icing along a mountain route on a windy winter day. What do you check first?
options: Whether the AIRMET and SIGMET overlays were turned off
Whether the TAF has a TEMPO group
The flight category colors
The Convective Outlook
final_quiz.why: GFA users can switch overlays such as AIRMETs and SIGMETs off, which can hide hazardous weather on the route [[28:471|AWH 28-2]].

final_quiz.q: The Day 3 Convective Outlook shows a SLGT area over your Saturday route. What is it forecasting?
options: General thunderstorms only
A slight risk of severe storms: tornadoes, gusts of 50 kt or more or hail 1 inch or larger
A Convective SIGMET will be issued
Storms covering 40% of the area
final_quiz.why: Outlook risk categories rate the potential for severe convection, defined as a tornado, gusts of 50 kt or more or hail 1 inch or larger; TSTM marks general storms [[28:457|AWH 27-56]].

final_quiz.q: The day after a cold front, cool air flows over warm, sunny ground. What weather do you teach your student to expect in the afternoon?
options: Stratus, fog and poor visibility
Cumulus clouds, bumpy air below them and good visibility
Smooth air and haze
Freezing drizzle
final_quiz.why: Air passing over a warmer surface becomes unstable: convective currents, cumulus, showers, turbulence and good surface visibility [[1:302|PHAK 12-18]]. Convective turbulence is under and in cumulus and usually smooth above [[28:234|AWH 19-2]].

final_quiz.q: The destination reports -RA BKN015 OVC030. Your student plans to fly VFR on top and descend through a hole. What do you teach?
options: Fine, rain means thin clouds
Expect clouds more than 4,000 ft thick, and do not go on top hoping for a hole
Fine if the TAF improves later
Only a problem at night
final_quiz.why: An airport reporting light or heavier precipitation suggests clouds more than 4,000 ft thick [[28:166|AWH 14-2]], and AC 91-92 warns against going on top hoping to find a hole [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

final_quiz.q: Ridge-level wind is forecast at 30 kt across a range in stable air. Your student plans to cross 1,000 ft above the ridge and descend on the lee side. Best teaching response?
options: Fine, the air is stable so it will be smooth
Expect strong downdrafts, turbulence and rotors near and below ridge level downwind; pick another route or day
Only a problem if lenticular clouds are visible
Fly faster to get through it
final_quiz.why: With 20 kt or more at ridge level expect moderate or greater turbulence, strong downdrafts and rotors [[28:242|AWH 19-10]]; rotors form near or below ridge level downwind [[28:199|AWH 16-10]], and stable air is what makes waves [[28:191|AWH 16-2]].

final_quiz.q: A METAR shows TSRA with a gust to 52 kt but no word "severe." What does the AIM say?
options: It is not severe unless the METAR says so
It meets the severe criteria because of the 50 kt or more wind
Severe needs hail of 1 inch or more
Severe needs a tornado
final_quiz.why: METARs have no severe thunderstorm descriptor, but a storm with 50 kt wind or 3/4 inch hail meets the severe criteria [[34:119|AIM 7-1-26]].

final_quiz.q: Your student will fly an airplane not certificated for icing. Cloud tops are 7,000 ft, the freezing level is 5,000 ft, and they plan VFR at 8,500 ft above the layer. What do you teach?
options: Fine, VFR on top avoids the ice
A descent through the cloud below 5,000 ft means icing, and the plan relies on finding a hole; do not go
Fine if the pitot heat works
Fine if the PIREPs report only light rime from jets
final_quiz.why: Expect icing in clouds at or below 0 °C [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]]; airplanes not certificated for icing must avoid it [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]]; and do not go on top hoping for a hole [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

final_quiz.q: Moist ocean air is moving inland over colder ground at 20 kt. Your student expects dense fog at the coast. What is more likely?
options: Radiation fog
Steam fog
Low stratus or stratocumulus, because wind above about 15 kt lifts advection fog
Clear skies
final_quiz.why: Advection fog deepens as the wind increases up to about 15 kt; stronger wind lifts it into low stratus or stratocumulus [[28:224|AWH 18-4]].

final_quiz.q: A controller says "moderate precipitation, one zero miles ahead" near building storms. What should your student understand?
options: The controller can see the turbulence in it
It means 26 to 40 dBZ; ATC radar cannot detect turbulence or clouds, and near storms turbulence can be far worse than the rain suggests
It means light rain only
It means the cell is over 20 miles away
final_quiz.why: Moderate is 26 to 40 dBZ, ATC radar cannot see clouds or turbulence, and near thunderstorms turbulence can be much greater than the precipitation intensity suggests [[34:97|AIM 7-1-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's numerical FRAT scores a low-risk "go," but a line of embedded thunderstorms crosses the route. How do you teach the FRAT result?
options: Trust the score; that is what the tool is for
A low score can hide one extreme risk; the storms alone can make it a no-go
Add points until it reaches the no-go line
Ignore the storms because they are embedded
final_quiz.why: Numerical FRATs should be used with caution: a single extreme hazard such as embedded storms can leave a low score that suggests "go" [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

takeaways: Teach where each product comes from and how old it is before you teach what it says.
Brief in the standard order, adverse conditions first, and update with an abbreviated briefing if the standard one is an hour old.
Reports are facts at a point; forecasts and advisories cover areas and carry uncertainty. No advisory does not mean no hazard.
For every K3 condition, teach the chain: product, meaning, action. Aim for correlation, not recitation.
Cockpit weather is strategic: 20 minutes or more ahead, and NEXRAD may be 15 to 20 minutes older than its label.
Personal minimums are set on the ground and never lowered for a specific flight; marginal in two categories means no-go.
Teach with demonstration-performance and close with a collaborative critique that ends in a decision.
cfi_notes: The ACS notes say the evaluator must assess at least three sub-elements if K2 or K3 is selected, and S2 needs three K3 conditions. Be ready on all twelve K3 items, not a favorite three.

Sources differ on severe hail size: the AIM uses 3/4 inch for Convective SIGMETs and severe thunderstorms (AIM 7-1-6, 7-1-26), while the SPC Convective Outlook uses 1 inch (AWH 27-56). Teach each in its own context.

Sources differ on NEXRAD age: AWH 3-2 says 5 to 15 minutes or more, while AIM 7-1-27, AWH 22-21, PHAK 13-19 and AC 91-92 7.7 say the weather may be 15 to 20 minutes older than the display. Teach the more conservative 15 to 20 minutes.
Fog and spread: AWH 18-2 says fog seldom forms above a 2 °C spread; AC 91-92 8.2 says be especially cautious at 3 °C or less. They do not conflict; use 3 °C as the planning flag.

Small differences in the numbers: PHAK 12-13 gives the moist adiabatic rate as 1.1 to 2.8 °C per 1,000 ft and AWH 12-3 as 1.2 to 3 °C; PHAK 12-20 gives cold front speed as 25 to 30 mph in one paragraph and 20 to 35 mph in another. AIM 7-1-6 lists AIRMET surface wind as greater than 30 kt while AWH 26-16 and AIM 7-1-4 say 30 kt or more. Students who read different books will ask; say why it does not change the decision.

Outdated lines: AC 91-74B (2015) still points to the ADDS website and says AIRMETs amend the area forecast, and the PHAK 2-18 example uses Flight Watch. The current AIM and AWH teach aviationweather.gov, the GFA (which replaced the legacy area forecast, AIM 7-1-4) and Flight Service. Teach the current system.

PHAK 13-21 says data-link weather is not limited by radio range; that describes satellite subscription services. FIS-B needs range and line of sight to a ground station (AIM 7-1-9). Find out which one your student's box uses.

Make external pressure real: role-play a passenger or client who pushes to go, and have the student say the no-go out loud with an alternative. The AIH checklist reminds that the more important the trip, the stronger the pull to compromise minimums.
If a student keeps canceling on good days, look for worry about the lesson itself (AIH 1-24), and do not let weather become the cover story.
gaps: The Ceiling and Visibility Analysis (CVA) product itself is not described in the AWH, AIM or PHAK; show the live product on aviationweather.gov and teach from the flight categories.
Installed weather radar, lightning detectors and EFB weather apps differ by model; the AIM and AWH send pilots to the manufacturer's guide for symbols, ranges and modes.
Expected local climate beyond the general notes (seasonal mountain waves, valley and coastal fog, summer convection) must come from local knowledge and local NWS products.
Icing certification, ice protection and any frost allowance for the training airplane come only from its POH/AFM.
The sources give a method and a sample for personal minimums, not the right numbers for a given student; those come from the student's own record and the instructor's judgment.

activities.title: Observation, analysis or forecast?
activities.intro: The AIM sorts weather information into three types. Sort each product.
activities.why: Observations are raw sensor data such as surface and airborne reports and radar; analyses interpret observed data; forecasts predict development and movement [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]]. In-flight advisories are forecasts [[34:68|AIM 7-1-6]], and the freezing level analysis is in the AWH Analysis chapter [[28:365|AWH 25-23]].

activities.title: Read the surface chart
activities.intro: Drag each label to the feature it names on the surface chart.
activities.why: Ridges are zigzag lines and troughs dashed lines [[28:349|AWH 25-7]]. Closely spaced isobars mean strong wind; widely spaced isobars mean light wind [[1:296|PHAK 12-12]].

activities.title: Work the numbers
activities.intro: Use the source formulas. Round as the question says.

items.q: Surface temperature 27 °C, dewpoint 19 °C. About how high (ft AGL) will cumulus bases form?
Surface temperature 68 °F, dewpoint 53 °F. Using the PHAK method, about how high (ft AGL) is the cloud base? Round to the nearest 100 ft.
The FB sample's 39,000 ft group is 750252. What wind speed (kt) is forecast?
items.why: 75 is more than 36, so subtract 50 from the direction (250°) and add 100 to the speed: 02 + 100 = 102 kt; the temperature is minus 52 °C because the sign is left off above 24,000 ft [[28:405|AWH 27-4]].

items.q: FB temperatures: 6,000 ft +03 and 9,000 ft -03. Assuming a steady lapse rate, about what is the freezing level (ft MSL)?
items.why: The temperature falls 6 °C in 3,000 ft, 2 °C per 1,000 ft. From +3 °C it reaches 0 after 3 / 2 x 1,000 = 1,500 ft: 6,000 + 1,500 = 7,500 ft. The FB gives the approximate freezing level [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]].

items.q: A station plot wind shaft has one pennant, two full barbs and one half barb. What is the wind speed (kt)?
items.why: Pennant 50, full barb 10, half barb 5 [[1:296|PHAK 12-12]]. 50 + 2 x 10 + 5 = 75 kt.

items.q: A student's baseline day VFR ceiling is the RMH sample, 2,500 ft. Tonight's trip is a night cross-country to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday. Using the RMH example adjustment, what ceiling (ft) applies?
items.why: The RMH example for this exact case adds 1,000 ft to the ceiling [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. 2,500 + 1,000 = 3,500 ft. (The sample baseline is a daytime value [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]; the RMH night baseline is higher, so a real plan would start there.)

activities.title: Learning levels and critique steps
activities.intro: Match each teaching term to what your student does.

pairs.r: Recites that fog seldom forms with a spread above 2 °C
Explains why a shrinking spread means rising humidity
Uses tonight's reports to predict fog at the destination by sunrise
Links the fog risk to a later departure and a different alternate
Retells the flight while you listen for gaps in the account
Says how the lesson will change their personal minimums

activities.why: Rote, understanding, application and correlation are the four practical learning levels [[25:65|AIH 3-14]] [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Replay and redirect are steps of the collaborative critique [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

activities.title: Put the standard briefing in order
activities.intro: Your student is about to self-brief. Put the standard briefing elements in the order Flight Service gives them. (The AWH allows adverse conditions and the synopsis to be combined.)
activities.why: The standard briefing runs adverse conditions, VFR flight not recommended when it applies, synopsis, current conditions, en route forecast, destination forecast, winds aloft, then NOTAMs and ATC delays [[28:26|AWH 3-3]] [[28:27|AWH 3-4]].

activities.title: True or false: cockpit weather
activities.intro: Your student makes these claims about weather in the airplane. True or false?

cards.s: FIS-B NEXRAD can be used to pick a safe gap between two cells.
cards.why: FIS products are not for tactical avoidance under about 3 minutes, such as finding a path through a hazard area [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]].

cards.s: A NEXRAD image labeled 4 minutes old may show weather 15 to 20 minutes older than that.
cards.why: The label gives the age of the mosaic, not of the weather in it [[1:329|PHAK 13-19]].

cards.s: Airborne weather radar will warn you of clear-air turbulence ahead.
cards.why: Airborne radar cannot detect clear-air turbulence [[28:276|AWH 22-21]].

cards.s: On airborne radar, a strong cell can hide another cell behind it.
cards.why: Attenuation: a cell can absorb or reflect all the signal, hiding cells behind it [[28:276|AWH 22-21]].

cards.s: FIS-B carries every NOTAM that a full preflight briefing includes.
cards.why: FIS-B may not include all the weather products or NOTAMs a preflight briefing does [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]].

cards.s: A controller who calls "heavy precipitation" can also tell you how rough it is inside.
cards.why: ATC radar cannot detect turbulence or clouds and calls all returns "precipitation" [[34:97|AIM 7-1-12]].

cards.s: Through a low-altitude-tier FIS-B radio you get regional NEXRAD but not the CONUS mosaic.
cards.why: Low-altitude-tier radios do not provide CONUS NEXRAD [[34:84|AIM TBL 7-1-4]].

activities.title: A summer dual cross-country, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are giving dual on a 120 NM summer cross-country. Your student makes the decisions and you coach. Choose what you would teach at each point.

steps.s: Day before: all week, air-mass thunderstorms have built over the route by about 1400 local and died out by early evening. Your student plans to depart at 1300 local for a 1 hour 20 minute flight.
options: Keep 1300; one hour of margin is enough
Depart early in the morning instead, landing long before the storms build, with an alternate planned
Depart at 1500 and use the NEXRAD to weave between cells
Cancel the trip for the whole week
steps.why: On days with afternoon thunderstorms forecast, an early morning departure (or waiting until they dissipate late in the day) reduces the risk [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]. AC 91-92 says not to plan flights in or near current or forecast convection [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

steps.s: Engine start is delayed; the standard briefing is now 90 minutes old.
options: It is still valid; a briefing lasts all day
Get an abbreviated briefing before takeoff
Get a new outlook briefing
Skip it; FIS-B will show any change
steps.why: Get an abbreviated briefing just before takeoff if the standard one is 1 hour or more old or the weather is questionable [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]]. FIS is not a substitute for a preflight briefing [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]].

steps.s: Midway, cumulus ahead is towering, and the display shows a growing cell 25 NM ahead and just left of course, label 4 minutes old.
options: Hold course and look at it when you get closer
Turn now to pass at least 20 miles from it, using the display to choose the whole route
Descend under the cloud base and keep going
Use the display to fly just right of the red
steps.why: Use data-link NEXRAD to avoid storms entirely, and avoid intense echoes by at least 20 miles [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]]. Decisions 20 minutes or more ahead are the strategic use FIS supports [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]].

steps.s: The destination now reports +TSRA with gusts to 35 kt. An airport 30 NM north is VFR.
options: Hold near the destination until the storm passes
Divert to the VFR airport and wait on the ground
Land quickly before it gets worse
Fly under the storm to the runway
steps.why: Do not land in the face of an approaching storm; if you cannot get around storms, divert and wait them out on the ground [[34:119|AIM 7-1-27]] [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]].

steps.s: Safely on the ground, you debrief. What method fits best?
options: A lecture listing every error
A collaborative critique: replay, reconstruct, reflect, redirect
No debrief; the flight ended safely
Score it with a numerical FRAT
steps.why: A collaborative critique uses open-ended questions so the learner assesses their own decisions before you compare views [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].
